subject: Geography
title: Plains and Rivers
learningOutcomes: Identify the physical features of plains and classify them by their type and by how they were formed.
Describe a river system and its parts, from source and tributaries to mouth, delta and distributaries.
Explain the three river processes — erosion, transportation and deposition — and where each dominates along the river's course.
Recognise and explain river landforms such as waterfalls, meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains, levees and deltas.
Evaluate the positive and negative impacts of rivers on people, farming and settlements.

sections.heading: Physical Features of Plains
sections.body: A plain is an extensive, nearly level stretch of land with little or no change in height or elevation. Plains are usually lower than the land around them and can be found along the coast or inland. They are often well-populated because the flat land is easy to build roads and railways on, and the soil is suitable for cultivation. The Indo-Gangetic Plain, formed by the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems, is the most populated region in the world and is home to one-seventh of the world's population. Its fertile alluvial soil — soil deposited by rivers over time — is the main reason so many people live there.

sections.heading: Types of Plains
sections.body: Plains can be classified by their physical features or by how they were formed. By features they include grasslands (like the Great Plains of North America), forested plains (the Tabasco Plain in Mexico), desert plains (parts of the Sahara) and tundra (frozen Arctic plains with only mosses and shrubs). By formation they are structural plains (formed when the ocean floor or continental shelf is uplifted), erosional plains or peneplains (worn down by denudation) and depositional plains. Depositional plains include alluvial, glacial (sandur and till), loess (wind-blown, like the Gobi), river, lava (dark because of basalt) and coastal plains. Abyssal plains lie thousands of metres below sea level on the ocean floor.

sections.heading: The River and Its System
sections.body: A river system is made up of the source, the main stream, tributaries, the mouth and distributaries. A river begins at its source in the highlands; as it flows, tributaries join it at points called confluences and the volume of water gradually increases. The mouth is where the river ends in a sea or lake, sometimes splitting into distributaries. The whole area drained by a river and its tributaries is its drainage basin, bounded by a watershed. A river's course has three parts: the upper course (steep gradient, small volume, rough bed), the middle course (gentler gradient, larger volume, meanders begin) and the lower course (almost flat, largest volume, smooth bed, deposition).

sections.heading: River Processes
sections.body: Rivers shape the land through three processes. Erosion wears away the channel and bed by abrasion (rock fragments scraping the bed), hydraulic action (water surging into cracks), solution (dissolving soluble minerals) and attrition (rocks colliding and becoming smaller and rounder). Vertical erosion deepens the channel in the upper course, while lateral erosion widens it in the middle and lower course. Transportation moves the load by traction (rolling heavy material), saltation (bouncing sand and pebbles), suspension (fine silt and clay carried in the water — most of the load) and solution (dissolved minerals). Deposition happens when the river loses energy: the heaviest boulders drop first and the finest silt travels furthest.

sections.heading: River Features
sections.body: A waterfall forms where a river flows over hard and soft rock; the soft rock erodes faster, the hard rock overhangs and collapses by undercutting, and a plunge pool forms at the base. Angel Falls in Venezuela (979 m) is the highest in the world. A meander is a bend in a river — erosion on the outer bank forms a steep river cliff, while deposition on the inner bank forms a gentle slip-off slope. When a meander's neck is cut off, a crescent-shaped oxbow lake is left behind. In the lower course the river builds floodplains and raised levees, and at its mouth it deposits sediment to form a delta — the Ganges Delta in Bangladesh is the largest in the world. A wide funnel-shaped mouth where fresh and sea water mix is an estuary.

sections.heading: Impacts of Rivers on People
sections.body: Rivers are vital to biodiversity and the economy. They provide water for irrigation and daily use, cheap and clean hydro-electric power, transport routes for people and goods, and food from fisheries. Fertile sediment deposited on floodplains constantly replenishes the soil, which is why river plains support such dense populations. Rivers are also highly productive ecosystems that support countless species. However, rivers can be harmful too: during the rainy season they overflow their banks and flood low-lying land, destroying homes, farmland and livestock, and sometimes costing lives. The Nile is the longest river in the world.

definitions.definition: An extensive, nearly level stretch of land with little change in height or elevation.
Fertile soil deposited by rivers over time, very good for growing crops.
The wearing away of the Earth's surface by rivers, rain, glaciers, ice and wind.
A smaller stream that flows into and joins the main river.
A smaller channel that branches out from the main river near its mouth.
The area of land drained by a river and all its tributaries.
The wearing away of the river channel and bed by the water and its load.
The dropping of the river's load when it loses energy and can no longer carry it.
A curve or bend in a river; erosion occurs on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank.
A flat landform at a river's mouth built up from deposited sediment.

examTips: Remember the order of a river's course: Upper (steep, erosion) → Middle (meanders) → Lower (flat, deposition).
Don't confuse a tributary (flows INTO the river) with a distributary (branches OUT near the mouth) — this is commonly tested.
Learn the outer bank of a meander = river cliff (erosion) and the inner bank = slip-off slope (deposition).
